newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Democrats duck Vrznitzky ultimatum.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Democrats duck Vrznitzky ultimatum.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party ducked European envoy Franz Vranitzky's ultimatum on Friday to sign a political contract on early elections, saying he wanted to talk about it further.

"I'm still thinking about it, I have another meeting with Mr Vranitzky," Democratic Party leader Tritan Shehu told Reuters as he arrived for the meeting with the European envoy at which the signing was due to have taken place.
Shehu, a former foreign minister, said he still had reservations about the six-point political contract Vranitzky asked the 10 Albanian parties to sign by 2 p.m. (1200 GMT).
Socialist leader Fatos Nano said he had signed the contract shortly after it was presented to the parties at a morning meeting.
"This is the last chance for us," he told reporters. "If they (the Democrats) don't sign it, they should expect lightning."

Vranitzky issued his ultimatum during his third visit since widespread rioting over failed pyramid savings schemes broke out in February. A former Austrian chancellor, he is now acting as envoy of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
The contract would commit the parties to holding general elections by the end of June under a mixed system of majority and proportional representation similar to that in force for elections in 1992.
It says a decision on the law should be taken by May 11.
The contract says the so-called salvation committees, citizens groups set up to restore order after the unrest, should be disbanded on or before the election date.
Every effort should be made to ensure free movement and access for all parties during the campaign.

The contract agrees to limit those banned from running in the election to former members of the Communist Political Bureau, state security police collaborators and people convicted of crimes against humanity.
This would free Socialist leader Fatos Nano, a senior communist official and former prime minister, to stand.
The contract also invites the international community to nominate a co-ordinator of international standing to make a final report on the electoral process, which the signatories would not contest.
"We are hopeful that our proposal will offer them a possibility to reach a compromise," Vranitzky's spokeswoman told Reuters before the envoy's meeting with the political parties.

President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party has been refusing to back down on its insistence that the existing electoral law, which allows for 25 seats in the 140-seat parliament to be chosen by proportional representation, be used for the June vote.
The democrats won 122 seats in the last election in May 1996. International observers said the result was seriously flawed and the opposition Socialists pulled out of the ballot late on polling day.

The Socialists of interim Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, as well as the seven other parties in the nine-party National Reconciliation Government, want a variation of the 1992 election law in which more seats were chosen by proportional representation.
The extra seats at issue would most likely go to minor parties in the government.

Fino has said the government will now adopt an electoral law by majority and pass it to parliament for approval. He has demanded a vote of confidence, and says the government will resign if the law is not passed.
Fino's spokesman said the prime minister would leave Tirana on Saturday for an official visit to Washington, stopping in Rome on the way to meet Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini.
